newsitem.title: LATVIA: Latvia welcomes S&P credit rating.
newsitem.headline: Latvia welcomes S&P credit rating.

text.p: Latvia is happy with Standard & Poor's (S&P) investment grade credit ratings, which should encourage more foreign funds to flow into the Baltic state, Prime Minister Andris Shkele said on Friday.
Latvia is the second Baltic country after Lithuania to get an international credit rating.
"It is a significant achievement," Shkele told a news conference. "I would call it a success. It provides the ground for modest but predictable foreign investment now."
Latvia, independent from the former Soviet Union since 1991, is expected to register gross domestic product (GDP) growth of around 2.5 percent for 1996 and year-on-year inflation of 13.1 percent.
Shkele came to power at the start of 1996 and has tried to speed economic reforms and privatisation.
"To be honest, I did not think a year's work would produce such a result, although it was included in my plans," said Shkele, also acting finance minister since last October.
S&P assigned Latvia a BBB rating for long-term foreign currency debt and single A-minus (A-) for long-term local currency debt.
Shkele last year pushed through a balanced 1997 budget for the first time in Latvia's history and it also met its 40 million lat budget deficit target for 1996.

Interest rates have continued to fall, with the central bank again reducing its key refinancing rate to nine percent in January and the average weighted yield for all government T-bills was below ten percent at the latest auction.
"It is good that we have the lowest investment grade ratings rather than the highest speculative grade ratings," Latvian stock exchange president Uldis Cerps told a news conference.
"This shows confidence in the policy of the Latvian central bank and in the lat, which is essential," he added.
